# Inclusive by Construction
## Cultural Design Guidance for a New Global Digital Product — Working Draft for the Product Council

**Version 1.0 — draft. Prepared for product council review, and for prior circulation to locale leads, Legal, Trust & Safety, and the accessibility guild. Not yet a specification.**

---

### How we would ask you to use this

One note, then the substance.

Most of what follows is written as **floors and hypotheses rather than rules**. The floors are the small number of things we think must hold in every market, because breaking them breaks the product for someone. Everything else is offered as a starting position that a locale owner is expected to mark up, contradict, or discard.

A locale checklist returned to us unamended will be read not as agreement but as a sign that nobody local has actually looked at it, and we would come back for it.

Two courtesies before this travels further. First, that §11 (legal and regulatory gates) is walked through with Group Legal and Privacy **before** any locale is committed to a launch date — the most expensive mistakes in this space are not offensive icons, they are data-residency and accessibility-law commitments discovered after the architecture has set. Second, that locale owners see §§3, 4 and 9 and have room to respond in their own way before the roadmap is frozen. A product about not imposing defaults that arrives in a market fully formed has already contradicted itself, and the people we most need to hear from will notice that first.

---

## 1. Recommendation on a page

**Build a thin universal core and a wide local expression: seven product invariants defined centrally as *floors*; everything else — copy register, imagery, iconography, payment rails, onboarding sequence, notification rhythm, even the product's name in market — devolved to locale owners; three instrumented launch locales chosen for maximum design distance from each other; and a published protocol binding the core team to the same discipline it asks of everyone else.**

| | |
|---|---|
| Universal floors | **Seven invariants** (§3) — no hardcoded human identity; locale data from a maintained source; text as data, never as pixels; direction-agnostic layout; no load-bearing colour or gesture; a named human appeal route for every automated decision; parity of function, not parity of appearance |
| Devolved to locales | Copy voice and formality register, imagery, iconography variants, payment methods, onboarding order, notification timing, feature sequencing, in-market naming |
| Launch shape | **Three instrumented locales** — one RTL, one CJK, one low-bandwidth/mobile-money-majority — deliberately different in design, identical in instrumentation (§10) |
| Principal risk | Not offence. **Silent exclusion** — the user who cannot enter their own name, cannot pay, or cannot read the screen, and who leaves without complaining (§7) |
| The core team's obligation | **Published override protocol**: the core may overrule a locale decision, but must give written reasons to the same people who saw the decision, and override counts are reported each quarter beside locale metrics (§9) |
| Measurement | Per-locale behavioural proxies weighted 70%, sentiment instruments 30%; never averaged across locales; acquiescence correction applied before any comparison is shown (§10) |
| Numeric failure test | Locale sentiment score rises ≥5 points while that locale's form-completion and time-to-first-value stay flat = declared failure of the localisation effort, not a success of it (§10.4) |
| Investment sought | **$4.6M Year 1, $2.9M Year 2** (illustrative, assumptions at §12.1), of which **$1.4M is paid in-market review time** — the line most often cut and most often fatal |
| Decisions requested | **Four** — §12.4 |
| Owner | Head of Product, sponsor; a named Localisation Architect appointed within 30 days, sitting in engineering, not in marketing |

### 1.1 The core proposition, and how confident we are in it

Cultural inclusion is overwhelmingly an **architecture** problem and only marginally a **content** problem. Products that get the architecture right can fix bad copy in an afternoon; products that get it wrong cannot fix a name field without a migration.

*(Considered practitioner assertion, not a research finding — see the evidence key at §13. We flag it because the council is entitled to know which statements here are evidenced and which are judgement.)*

The specific failure we are trying to avoid is well documented in our own past work: a product shipped as an American product with a language dropdown bolted to it, then patched market by market until the codebase carries forty conditional branches nobody understands. That outcome is worse than launching in fewer markets, because it consumes the engineering credibility a second attempt would need.

---

## 2. Diagnosis before we design

### 2.1 A framing we would gently ask the council to test

The brief describes this as ensuring the product "does not offend". The evidence available to us suggests offence is the *smallest* of the four risks, and the only one that generates visible feedback.

| Candidate driver | What "cultural sensitivity review" does to it |
|---|---|
| Data model assumes one shape of name, address, family, gender | Nothing — requires schema change before launch |
| Locale data hardcoded rather than sourced from CLDR | Nothing — requires engineering standard, not review |
| Layout cannot survive text expansion or right-to-left | Nothing — requires CSS/layout discipline from first commit |
| Copy carries idiom, humour, sports metaphor, US legal register | **Improves substantially** — this is what review is good at |
| Iconography carries culture-specific gestures or objects | Improves, *if* paired with a funded variant library |
| Payment, identity and connectivity assumptions exclude whole markets | Nothing — requires commercial and infrastructure decisions |
| ML systems trained on skewed data mis-serve non-majority users | Worsens — a review that passes it lends it false legitimacy |
| Moderation policy written in one legal and moral idiom | Worsens — a global policy applied locally reads as foreign rule |

Only one row responds to the intervention most companies actually fund. We would rather establish which rows we have before committing the budget.

### 2.2 The diagnostic we propose

Four weeks, running in parallel with early architecture, no design freeze until it reports:

- **Schema stress test.** Attempt to register and transact as sixteen constructed personas — an Indonesian mononym, an Icelandic patronymic, a Spanish two-surname, a Japanese user needing phonetic name fields, a user with no postal code, a user with a nine-digit phone number, a user on a shared household device, a user whose legal sex and daily identity differ, and eight more. Record every point of hard failure.
- **Pseudo-localisation build.** Run the entire UI through machine pseudo-translation with +40% text expansion and full bidi mirroring. Screenshot every screen. Count breakages.
- **Connectivity and device audit.** Load the product on a sub-$100 Android device over a throttled 3G connection with a metered data plan. Record time-to-first-interaction and total payload.
- **Six in-market conversations per launch locale**, with people who are not employees.

Cost **$180K**. It is the cheapest consequential decision in this programme, and if it finds that the data model is the binding constraint, most of the Year 1 content budget should be redirected to schema and layout work before anything is committed.

### 2.3 The uncomfortable question, answered rather than deferred

Will the core team be bound by the same rules? If locale owners discover that the core reserves the right to overturn their decisions without giving reasons — or that "global consistency" is invoked selectively, and always in the direction of the headquarters market — the guidance becomes decoration and everything downstream of it is wasted. **§9 answers this with a specific, testable, reportable mechanism**, and we would ask the council to adopt or amend it rather than to note it.

---

## 3. What is fixed everywhere: seven invariants, stated as floors

Framed as what the *product* must not do, rather than as what designers must do, so that very different designs can honour them.

### 3.1 Invariant I — no hardcoded assumptions about human identity

**Floor:** the system must be able to store and display any person's name, address, phone number, family structure and identity without loss, truncation, transliteration or refusal.

| Element | Specification |
|---|---|
| Name | One required field: `full_name`, Unicode, minimum 100 characters, no character-class validation beyond a length and control-character check. Optional: `display_name` (what we call you), `phonetic_name` (Japan, and useful elsewhere), `sort_key`. **No required first/last split.** Never infer gender, ethnicity or seniority from a name |
| Name ordering | Store an explicit `name_order` hint; default from locale but always user-overridable. Never reorder for display without it |
| Address | Locale-driven field sets sourced from CLDR / an address-format library. Postal code, state and county are **optional by default** and required only where the locale data says so. Free-form fallback line always available |
| Phone | E.164 storage, no fixed-length validation, international dialling permitted from every locale |
| Gender | **Three separate concepts, never conflated**: legal sex (collected only where a named legal requirement exists, and the requirement is cited in code comments), gender identity (optional, extensible, with prefer-not-to-say), and honorific/salutation (optional, locale-extensible, and skippable) |
| Pronouns & grammatical gender | Copy generated with ICU `select` on a user-set gender token, never string concatenation. Where a language's inclusive-form debate is live and unsettled, that decision belongs to the locale owner, not the core (§4.3) |
| Family & relationships | No assumption of two-parent, two-person, or single-household structures in any flow that models relationships |
| Age | Date-of-birth collection minimised; where legally required, remember the digital-consent age varies by jurisdiction (13–16 across the EU alone) |

### 3.2 Invariant II — locale data comes from a maintained source, never from a developer's memory

**Floor:** no formatting logic for dates, times, numbers, currency, sorting, pluralisation or measurement units may be written by hand. All of it derives from Unicode CLDR via ICU, at runtime, from the user's chosen locale.

This is the single highest-leverage engineering standard in the document, and it costs almost nothing if adopted in week one.

| Trap | What CLDR/ICU handles that hand-rolled code does not |
|---|---|
| Plurals | Six plural categories in Arabic; Polish and Russian *few*/*many*; Welsh; Japanese with none. `if (n == 1)` is wrong in most of the world |
| Digit grouping | Indian 2-2-3 grouping (lakh/crore) vs Western 3-3-3; space vs comma vs period separators |
| Currency | Zero-decimal (JPY, KRW), three-decimal (KWD, BHD, OMR), symbol placement, rounding rules |
| Calendars | Hijri, Hebrew, Buddhist Era (+543, Thailand), Japanese imperial eras, Republic-of-China era (Taiwan), Persian Jalali, Indian national calendar |
| Week structure | Week starts Monday, Sunday or Saturday depending on locale; weekend is Fri–Sat, Sat–Sun, or Saturday alone depending on country — and this changes (the UAE moved in 2022) |
| Time | 12- vs 24-hour clocks; southern-hemisphere DST is inverted; several countries have none |
| Collation | Swedish å ä ö sort after z; German ä may sort as *a* or *ae* depending on context; Chinese by pinyin or by stroke count |
| Measurement | Units, paper sizes, first day of fiscal year, address ordering |

**Storage rule:** UTC and ISO 8601 internally, always. Locale formatting at the presentation layer only.

### 3.3 Invariant III — text is data, never pixels

**Floor:** no user-visible text may be baked into an image, an icon, a video overlay or a hardcoded string. Every string carries a translator note giving context, character budget and whether it is a verb or a noun.

Corollaries, all cheap now and expensive later:
- **No sentence assembly by concatenation.** Word order is not universal. Use full-sentence ICU messages with named placeholders.
- **Design for +40% expansion and −30% contraction.** German, Finnish and Russian run long; CJK runs short. Layouts that only work at English length will break in Berlin before they break anywhere exotic.
- **Font stacks must cover the scripts we ship.** Noto or equivalent, with tested

# Global Employee Empowerment & Adaptive Culture Initiative
## Guidance on Regional Leadership Adaptation — Recommendation for Sponsor Group

**Version 2.0 — complete. Prepared for sponsor group decision, and for prior circulation to the fourteen regional people leads. Not yet for employee communication.**

---

### How we would ask you to use this

One note only, and then the substance.

This version differs from v1.0 in three ways that the reviewers were right to insist on. It now asks for specific decisions, with money and a date attached (§12). It answers the questions the first draft deferred — most importantly what the centre itself is bound by (§9). And the regional material has been re-cut so that no colleague opens it and finds their country described inside someone else's card.

The regional cards in §6 remain what they were: **working hypotheses, offered so that they can be corrected**. Where a region has its own diagnostic data, that data replaces the card and the card is retired for that unit (§5.4). A card returned to us unamended will be read not as agreement but as a sign that the conversation has not yet taken place, and we would come back for it.

Two courtesies we would ask the sponsor group to extend before this travels further. First, that the fourteen regional people leads and the four regional MDs see §§3, 4 and 9 and have time to respond in their own way before the board pack is assembled — a programme about devolved authority that arrives in a region fully formed has already contradicted itself, and colleagues will notice that before they notice anything else. Second, that §10 (consultation and legal gates) be walked through with Group Legal, the European Works Council secretariat and Group Reward before any part of this is described to employees anywhere. The likeliest single cause of avoidable damage is a well-intentioned announcement that reaches a works council after it reaches a newspaper, or reaches an employee before it reaches their own supervisor.

---

## 1. Recommendation on a page

**Adopt a thin global core and a wide local expression: four employee entitlements defined centrally as *floors*, with a formal alternative-form process where a floor cannot lawfully or structurally be met; delivery method, language, sequencing and naming devolved entirely to regions; four instrumented pilots in Year 1 with a common measurement spine but deliberately different local design; and a published protocol binding the centre to the same discipline it asks of others.**

| | |
|---|---|
| Global mandate | **Four entitlements only** (§3) — decision rights at the lowest competent level; an answered route for dissent; tolerance of good-faith error; employee-initiated internal movement. Each stated as a floor, each with a named-approver alternative-form route (§3.6) |
| Devolved to regions | Language, ritual, sequencing, symbolism, manager incentives, pace, communication channels, and the programme's name. We would suggest the centre resist standardising even the name |
| Year 1 shape | **Four pilots — one high-authority-distance, one low, one deskless-majority, one recently-acquired entity** — different in design, identical in instrumentation (§7) |
| Principal risk | Middle-manager status and grade loss, not employee resistance (§8) |
| The centre's own obligation | **Published reversal protocol**: the centre may reverse a devolved decision, but must give written reasons to the same audience that saw the decision, and reversal counts are reported quarterly beside regional metrics (§9) |
| Measurement | Within-region trend on four behavioural proxies weighted 70%, survey items 30%; acquiescence correction applied before any cross-region view is shown (§8.3) |
| Numeric failure test | Empowerment survey index +5 points or more while decision latency on the instrumented decision class improves <10% and internal-move rate is flat = declared failure, programme paused, no further capital (§8.5) |
| Investment sought | **$14.2M Year 1, $10.6M Year 2** (illustrative, assumptions in §12.1), of which $6.9M is manager time relief — the line most often omitted and most often fatal |
| Funding split | Central P&L funds diagnostic, instrumentation, platform, central team and pilot facilitation; regions fund manager time with a **60% central offset in Y1, 30% in Y2, nil thereafter** (§12.3) |
| Decisions requested | **Three** — §12.5, sought at the sponsor group meeting on **18 March** |
| Programme owner | Group Chief People Officer, sponsor; named programme director recruited internally within 30 days of approval |

### 1.1 The core proposition, and how confident we are in it

Empowerment mechanisms do not transfer between contexts; the conditions that make them work can be built in each. *(This is our considered assertion from practitioner experience, not a finding — see the evidence key at §14. We flag it because the sponsor group is entitled to know which of our statements are evidenced and which are judgement.)*

The specific failure we are trying to avoid is well documented in our own past programmes: exported behavioural vocabulary — "speak up", "own it", "disagree and commit" — produces regions that become fluent at the annual survey and unchanged on Tuesday morning. That outcome is worse than no initiative, because it consumes the credibility a second attempt would require.

---

## 2. Diagnosis before we design

### 2.1 The framing we would gently ask the sponsor group to test

The initiative is currently described as culture change. The evidence available to us may instead describe a **decision-rights and information-flow** problem wearing culture-change clothing. Only one of those two responds to leadership behaviour work, and we would rather establish which we have before committing eight figures to the wrong one.

| Candidate driver | What leadership/empowerment training does to it |
|---|---|
| Decision rights formally held too high | Nothing — requires delegation-of-authority redesign |
| Rights delegated on paper, retracted in practice | Nothing until retraction is made visible and costly (§9) |
| Information does not reach the level holding authority | **Amplifies harm** — confident decisions on poor data |
| Managers lack coaching capability | Improves, *if* paired with funded time relief (§8.4) |
| Reward and grading pay for control, not for developing others | Nothing — the incentive wins every time (§8.2) |
| Employees have voice but no evidence it is ever acted on | Worsens — a further unanswered invitation deepens cynicism |
| Working-language barrier suppresses contribution | Nothing — needs channel design, not confidence-building (§11.1) |

### 2.2 The diagnostic we propose

Five weeks, no design freeze until it reports: 60 structured conversations across four organisational levels in eight countries (including two deskless-majority sites); an audit of the documented delegation-of-authority matrix against actual practice in twelve units; and a language-barrier check in the four sites where the working language is not the local one. Cost **$310K**.

If it finds that decision rights are formally too high, the largest part of the Year 2 training envelope should be redirected to delegation architecture and the pilot scope revised before commitment. This is the cheapest consequential decision in the programme.

### 2.3 The uncomfortable question, now answered rather than deferred

Will headquarters be bound by the same four entitlements? If regional colleagues discover that the centre reserves the right to overturn devolved decisions without giving reasons, the initiative becomes rhetoric and everything downstream of it is wasted. v1.0 left this open. **§9 now answers it with a specific, testable, reportable mechanism**, and we would ask the sponsor group to adopt or amend it rather than to note it.

---

## 3. What is fixed everywhere: four entitlements, stated as floors

Framed as what an employee is entitled to, not as how a manager must behave, so that very different conduct can honour them.

### 3.1 Entitlement I — decision rights sit at the lowest competent level
**Floor:** every employee can name the classes of decision they own and point to a recent instance of exercising one without seeking permission. *Competent* is doing real work in that sentence; this is not an argument for uniform flat structures.

### 3.2 Entitlement II — there is a route for dissent, and it is answered
**Floor:** every employee has at least one available channel through which they can contradict a superior's view **and receive a response**. The channel may be a written pre-read, a skip-level, a facilitated small group, a mentor, a shift huddle, or an anonymous board. It need never be a raised hand in a large meeting. The answered part is the floor; the form is entirely local.

**Firewall, mandatory:** this channel is expressly **not** a statutory reporting channel. Disagreement about a business decision is not a protected disclosure. The two must be separately named, separately routed and separately governed, or we create legal exposure on one side and chill genuine reporting on the other (§10.3).

### 3.3 Entitlement III — good-faith error is absorbed, not attributed
**Floor:** within each unit, at least one specific, visible instance per quarter in which a good-faith mistake was absorbed rather than attributed, and the team can name it. Demonstrated, never announced. In several regions this must be framed collectively rather than individually to be usable at all (§6).

### 3.4 Entitlement IV — employees can initiate their own movement
**Floor (revised from v1.0):** an employee may apply for an internal role, project or rotation **without the incumbent manager holding a veto and without the manager being informed in advance of the application**.

v1.0 stated this as an absolute and was wrong to. In parts of the Gulf, mobility between entities is constrained by employer-tied work permits and is a legal matter, not a cultural one. In Japan, Korea and Taiwan, seniority-anchored career and reward structures make unrestricted lateral self-nomination structurally disruptive in ways that a global mandate cannot responsibly overrule from a distance. The floor above is the most we can hold everywhere; where even that cannot be met, §3.6 applies.

### 3.5 Everything else is regional property
Language, ceremony, sequencing, symbolism, tooling, incentives, cadence, and the programme's own name.

### 3.6 The alternative-form process (in place of exemption)

We deliberately avoid the word *exemption*, and avoid asking any region to refuse. A region that cannot meet a floor is asked instead to **propose the nearest form it can honour**, and to say what it would take to close the remainder.

| Element | Provision |
|---|---|
| Trigger | Legal impossibility, collective-agreement conflict, or structural impossibility (not difficulty, not discomfort) |
| Form | Two pages: which floor, why, the alternative mechanism proposed, and the condition under which the floor becomes reachable |
| Approver | **Group Chief People Officer**, countersigned by the Regional MD and by Group Legal |
| Duration | **12 months maximum**, renewable once with fresh reasoning |
| Visibility | Entered in an internally published register, reviewed quarterly by the sponsor group |
| Presumption | An alternative form is accepted unless it is materially weaker than the floor. We expect four to eight across the network in Year 1 and would be suspicious of zero |

---

## 4. The adaptation logic

### 4.1 Four variables, rather than a general culture model

We would ask each region to place itself on four axes only, because these four determine whether a given mechanism functions or backfires.

| Axis | The question | What it changes |
|---|---|---|
| **Authority basis** | Does a manager's authority derive from role or from demonstrated expertise? | Whether devolution reads as trust or as abandonment |
| **Directness of disagreement** | Can dissent be public without cost to either party? | The design of the dissent channel (Entitlement II) |
| **Attribution of error** | Does a mistake attach to a person, a team, or a system? | Whether error tolerance can be individual or must be collective (III) |
| **Ambiguity tolerance** | Is an open brief experienced as freedom, or as information withheld? | How much structure must accompany autonomy |

### 4.2 The working rule

> High authority distance and low disagreement-directness do not mean empowerment is unwelcome. They mean it must be **granted rather than seized** — granted visibly, specifically, bounded, and by someone whose authority the team already accepts.

In such contexts an open invitation ("bring me your ideas") is not empowerment; it is a test most colleagues will decline to sit. The functioning equivalent is a named, bounded, publicly conferred mandate: *"Priya decides this class of exception up to this threshold. She does not need to ask me. If you disagree with her, take it to her."* Our practitioner judgement is that this single act moves more behaviour than a quarter of workshops — offered as judgement, not as measured finding (§14), and testable inside the pilots via the decision-latency proxy.

### 4.3 Sponsorship: a default with a visible opt-out

**Default:** regional sponsors are selected on observed practice — leaders whose own teams already exhibit the four entitlements — rather than on rank.

We acknowledged in v1.0 that this backfires in several regions, then handed the choice back, which was no recommendation at all. The corrected position: the default stands, and a region wishing to depart from it does so through a **one-page note countersigned by the Regional MD and the programme director**, logged in the same register as §3.6. Departures are expected and unremarkable; what matters is that they are visible.

Where the practitioner sponsor sits two or three levels below the Regional MD, the workable form is almost always a **pair** — the senior figure as visible patron providing cover and air, the practitioner as the working engine. A junior sponsor without a senior patron will in several regions be read, reasonably, as the centre not taking the region seriously.

---

## 5. Using the regional cards well

### 5.1 What they are
Starting hypotheses about context, to be returned marked up within 45 days. They describe patterns we have observed in workplaces, not peoples.

### 5.2 What each card contains
Working hypothesis on the four axes · where the gap likely sits · behaviour to add · behaviour to drop · failure mode · **leading indicator observable by day 60** · legal or structural watch item.

### 5.3 The 60-day indicator, and why it is on every card
The failure modes that matter most — courteous non-adoption, affirmative response with no movement — are precisely the ones you cannot detect by asking. Each card therefore names an observable proxy visible within 60 days.

### 5.4 The supersession rule
**Where unit-level diagnostic data exists, it supersedes the card, and the card is retired for that unit.** Within-country variance in work values routinely exceeds between-country variance; function, site history and acquisition lineage frequently dominate nationality. This applies to every card, not only where we have noted it.

### 5.5 Scope note
Cards cover the fourteen clusters where we have wholly-owned or majority-controlled operations. Russia and Belarus are **out of scope** for this programme pending the Group's standing position on those entities; the programme director should not open a workstream there without a written instruction from the sponsor group.

---

## 6. Regional cards

### Card A — Anglosphere (US, Canada, UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand)

| | |
|---|---|
| Working hypothesis | Low authority distance; direct disagreement acceptable; individual error attribution; moderate-to-high ambiguity tolerance |
| Likely gap | Not permission — **follow-through**. Voice is already loud; evidence that it changes anything is thin |
| Add | Visible closure loops: "here is what we did with what you told us, here is what we declined, and why" |
| Drop | Announcing empowerment. The region has heard it and discounts it |
| Failure mode | Ironic compliance; strong survey movement, unchanged decision latency |
| 60-day indicator | Ratio of raised items with a documented, dated response — target 80%+; skip-level uptake |
| Watch item | Strong individual error attribution and litigation exposure make Entitlement III hard: blame follows the name. US at-will/discipline documentation practice cuts against visible error absorption |
| Internal variance not to flatten | UK indirectness is closer to the Nordic-plus-hedging pattern than to US directness; Quebec sits closer to Card C than to the rest of Canada; the Australian register tolerates challenge to authority that would be career-limiting in the US |

### Card B — Germanic & Nordic (DE, AT, CH, NL, SE, DK, NO, FI)

| | |
|---|---|
| Working hypothesis | Low-to-moderate authority distance, expertise-derived; very direct disagreement; system-oriented error attribution; **low ambiguity tolerance** |
| Likely gap | Vagueness. Autonomy without written scope reads as management failure, not freedom |
| Add | Precision — documented decision rights, thresholds, escalation triggers. More documentation produces more autonomy here, counter-intuitively |
| Drop | Motivational framing and aspirational language; actively corrosive of credibility |
| Failure mode | Formal structural objection: "not properly specified, and it touches co-determination" — and they will be right on both counts |
| 60-day indicator | Existence of a signed, unit-level decision-rights schedule; count of decisions taken against it |
| Watch item | **Works councils** — Betriebsrat, ondernemingsraad, Nordic union structures. Changes to appraisal criteria, working methods and monitoring are frequently co-determination matters. Engage as co-designers, not as clearance (§10.2) |
| Quiet opportunity | This cluster will build the best delegation architecture in the network. We would suggest letting it lead the design and having other regions borrow from it, rather than the reverse — a small reversal of the usual flow that would itself say something useful about the initiative |

### Card C — Latin Europe (FR, IT, ES, PT, GR)

| | |
|---|---|
| Working hypothesis | Moderate-to-high authority distance; direct on substance, relationship-mediated in form; individual attribution with strong reputational weight; moderate ambiguity tolerance |
| Likely gap | Relational legitimacy. It must come from a leader people are personally loyal to, or it is noise from the centre |
| Add | Public named conferral (§4.

- Country/territory pickers and the flags-as-language-selectors anti-pattern
- Imagery and representation: skin tone, dress, family composition, gesture (thumbs-up, OK sign, open palm, beckoning), alcohol/pork/exposed skin, physical contact between genders
- Colour semantics (white and mourning; red; green), number avoidance (4 in CJK, 13, 39 in Afghanistan)
- Humour, idiom, sports metaphor, seasonal assumptions ("spring cleaning" in Sydney), religious references, holiday calendars
- Translation governance: glossary/termbase, do-not-translate lists, MT/LLM post-editing standards, back-translation for high-risk strings, tone-and-formality registers (T/V distinction, keigo levels)
- Content moderation policy localisation — flagged as a "worsens" row in §2.1, then never addressed
- User-generated-content translation and in-language reporting/appeal flows

**3. Almost no *features* are proposed.** The brief asked for them. Candidates the draft should name concretely: language preference decoupled from country/region format preference; user-selectable calendar and numeral system; name-pronunciation audio and phonetic fields exposed to other users; script-aware search and transliterated matching; RTL/LTR mixed-content handling in user input; timezone and working-week-aware scheduling and notification quiet hours; "report a translation error" affordance on every screen; in-language human support routing; caption/alt-text in the user's language; offline and SMS fallback paths; low-literacy mode (icon + audio + reduced text).

---

## B. Substantive analytical gaps

**4. Devolution is asserted without a variability-management strategy, and it contradicts the document's own stated failure mode.**
§1.1 says the disaster to avoid is "forty conditional branches nobody understands." §1 then devolves onboarding order, feature sequencing, notification timing, payment rails, iconography variants and in-market naming to locale owners. That is a recipe for exactly forty conditional branches unless variation is *data-driven and bounded* — config/CMS/feature-flag-declared, with a named cap on the variation surface, a deprecation process for locale forks, and per-locale QA cost owned by the locale that requested the fork. The draft needs a "how variation is expressed" section or the whole devolution thesis is an unfunded liability on engineering.

**5. No safety analysis of the identity data it recommends collecting.**
§3.1 recommends optional gender-identity capture. In several markets that data endangers users (criminalisation, family disclosure on shared devices, government data requests). The floor should be *data minimisation with jurisdictional suppression and local-only storage*, not "optional, extensible." The draft also raises "shared household device" in the diagnostic personas and then never carries it into a design principle (private modes, notification content suppression, profile switching).

**6. Human-rights and legal-conflict cases are unaddressed.**
What happens when a floor is unlawful or unsafe locally — data-residency mandates (China PIPL, India DPDP, Russia, Nigeria, Indonesia, Vietnam), real-name registration requirements, censorship demands, or accessibility law? The employee-empowerment predecessor had an explicit "alternative form" process; this draft has floors with no exception mechanism at all. That is a regression, not a simplification.

**7. AI/ML fairness is diagnosed and then dropped.**
§2.1 says ML skew "worsens" under review — correct and important — but no invariant covers it. It needs one: disaggregated evaluation by language/script/region before launch; documented non-English performance floors for any NLP, speech, OCR, face or fraud-risk model; explicit prohibition on name-, address- or language-derived risk features; and the appeal route (Invariant VI) wired to it.

**8. Accessibility is name-checked, not designed.**
The brief said "inclusive **and accessible**." The draft mentions an accessibility guild and "no load-bearing colour," and stops. Missing: a stated conformance target (WCAG 2.2 AA), the regulatory gates that make it non-negotiable and dated (European Accessibility Act, EN 301 549, ADA Title II rule, national equivalents), assistive-technology test matrix, and the interaction between accessibility and localisation (screen-reader language tagging, `lang` attributes on mixed-script content, reading order in RTL, font fallback breaking AT pronunciation).

**9. China is filed under "CJK."** Treating China as a script/typography locale is a category error. It is an app-store, ICP-licensing, payments, identity-verification, hosting and partnership problem before it is a typography problem. Either name it as its own decision or explicitly scope it out — do not let it hide in a launch-locale bucket.

**10. No benefit case.** $4.6M is requested with the assumptions section missing. A product council will ask: which markets does this unlock, what conversion lift is expected in the three launch locales, what remediation and re-platforming cost is avoided, what regulatory exposure is retired? Absent that, the $1.4M in-market review line the draft calls "most often cut" will be cut again.

---

## C. Technical errors and imprecision

| Item | Problem |
|---|---|
| `full_name` "minimum 100 characters" | Unspecified unit — bytes, code points, or grapheme clusters? Specify grapheme clusters and a byte ceiling; 100 code points is short for some South Indian and Arabic full names |
| "No character-class validation beyond a length and control-character check" | Under-secure. Must also mandate Unicode normalisation (NFC) on storage and comparison, stripping/neutralising bidi override characters (U+202A–U+202E, U+2066–U+2069), and a confusables/homoglyph policy for display names. "Control character" does not cover these |
| Case handling | Absent, and it is the classic bug: Turkish dotless ı, German ß→SS, Greek final sigma. Mandate locale-aware casing or, better, no automated casing of user content at all |
| E.164 "no fixed-length validation" | E.164 has a 15-digit maximum; the right rule is "validate against a maintained numbering-plan library (libphonenumber), never a regex" |
| "Text as data, never pixels" | Needs carve-outs and rules for wordmarks/logos (which themselves need script variants), SVG-embedded text, canvas/WebGL rendering, and mandatory alt text — as written, the invariant will fail QA on legitimate cases and be quietly ignored |
| Locale ≠ language ≠ region | Never stated. Users routinely want UI in language A with formats from region B (`zh-Hans-SG`, an English UI with Indian numbering). The model must separate UI language, format locale, currency and timezone as four independent user settings with sensible fallback chains |
| Invariant V bundling | "No load-bearing colour or gesture" fuses an accessibility rule with a cultural rule. Different rationales, different tests, different owners — split them |
| CLDR table | Good, but missing: locale fallback chains, non-Gregorian *input* (not just display), Eastern Arabic and Devanagari numeral display, and the fact that "week starts on" and "weekend is" are separate CLDR fields |

*(Note: the persona count in §2.2 is internally consistent — eight listed plus eight more equals sixteen. No error there.)*

---

## D. Method and measurement weaknesses

**11. The 70/30 weighting is unjustified and sits oddly beside "never averaged across locales."** If cross-locale averaging is forbidden, what is the 70/30 composite *for*? Either drop the weighting or state what decision it drives.

**12. "Acquiescence correction applied" is a promise without a method.** Name it — within-respondent standardisation, anchoring vignettes, or forced-choice item design — or delete it. As written it invites the council to believe a comparability problem has been solved when it has not.

**13. The failure test is clever but toothless.** "Sentiment +5 while completion and TTFV flat = declared failure" has no observation window, no baseline variance, no sample-size floor, no statistical test, and — critically — **no consequence**. The predecessor document at least attached "programme paused, no further capital." Here failure is merely *declared*. Attach a trigger.

**14. The cheapest, most diagnostic metrics are missing.** Per-field form-error and abandonment rates by locale; name-field rejection counts; funnel drop-off by script; support-ticket taxonomy by locale; app-store review mining by language; payment-failure reasons by country; uninstall within 24 hours on sub-$100 devices. These are available in week one and would make the whole measurement section concrete.

**15. Six in-market conversations per locale, with three locales, is eighteen conversations for a $4.6M programme.** Too thin to detect anything but the obvious, and the draft elsewhere insists (correctly) that the dangerous failures are silent. Either raise it or reposition it honestly as colour rather than evidence.

---

## E. Form and voice

**16. The document is a structural transplant from an unrelated deliverable.** "One note, then the substance"; "Two courtesies before this travels further

# Inclusive by Construction
## Cultural Design and Accessibility Guidance for a New Global Digital Product

**Version 2.0 — complete, and prepared for decision. For the Product Council, and for circulation to locale owners, Group Legal & Privacy, Trust & Safety, and the accessibility guild before the roadmap is frozen. Not yet a public or customer-facing artefact.**

---

### Reading note

This version exists because reviewers of v1.0 were right on almost every count, and it is better that we say so plainly at the front than let colleagues discover it later.

Three things have changed. The invariants are now all specified rather than named — there are **ten** rather than seven, because two of the original seven bundled an accessibility rule with a cultural rule and had to be separated, and because algorithmic fairness and user-safety were diagnosed in v1.0 and then quietly dropped (§3). There is now a **content guidelines** half to the document (§7) and a **named feature set** (§6), which the brief asked for and v1.0 did not supply. And the document now commits: the override protocol is written and adoptable (§10), the money has assumptions and a benefit case attached (§14), and there are five specific decisions (§15).

Two requests on process, offered in the hope they save us all difficulty later.

The first is that locale owners see §§3, 4, 5 and 10 and have unhurried room to respond in their own manner — in writing, in conversation, or through their regional lead, whichever suits them — before the roadmap is frozen. A document about not imposing defaults that arrives in a market already settled has contradicted itself, and the colleagues we most need to hear from will notice that before they notice anything else.

The second is that §12 (legal, regulatory and consultation gates) is walked through with Group Legal and Privacy **before any launch date is committed to any market**. Our experience is that the expensive mistakes in this area are not offensive icons. They are data-residency architecture, accessibility statute, and platform-store policy discovered after the schema has set and the date has been announced. An icon can be changed in an afternoon without anyone losing face; a re-platforming cannot.

Everything in §§6, 7 and 9 is offered as a **starting position to be marked up, contradicted or discarded** by the people who know each market. A locale checklist returned to us unamended will be read not as agreement but as a sign that the conversation has not yet happened, and we would come back for it rather than proceed.

---

## 1. Recommendation on a page

**Build a thin universal core and a wide local expression: ten product invariants defined centrally as *floors*, with a formal alternative-form route where a floor cannot lawfully or safely be met; copy register, imagery, iconography, payment rails, onboarding sequence, notification rhythm and in-market naming devolved to locale owners — but expressed as bounded configuration, never as forked code; three instrumented launch locales chosen for maximum design distance; and a published protocol binding the core team to the same discipline it asks of everyone else.**

| | |
|---|---|
| Universal floors | **Ten invariants** (§3): identity data model · locale data from a maintained source · text as data · direction- and script-agnostic layout · accessibility conformance (WCAG 2.2 AA) · no load-bearing culture-specific signal · algorithmic parity across languages and scripts · a named human appeal route in the user's language · data minimisation and safety by default · parity of function, not appearance |
| Exception route | **Alternative form, not exemption** (§4). A locale that cannot meet a floor proposes the nearest form it can honour, and states what would close the gap. Approved by Head of Product, countersigned by Legal. We expect three to six in Year 1 and would be suspicious of zero |
| Devolved to locales | Copy voice and formality register, imagery, iconography variants, payment methods, onboarding order, notification timing, feature sequencing, in-market naming — all **declared in configuration and content, within a capped variation surface** (§5) |
| Launch shape | **Three instrumented locales** — one RTL (Arabic, Gulf or Egypt), one Japan, one low-bandwidth / mobile-money-majority (Indonesia or Kenya) — deliberately different in design, identical in instrumentation (§11) |
| China | **Not a locale. A separate decision** (§13), and one we would ask the council to take explicitly rather than let it hide inside "CJK" |
| Principal risk | Not offence. **Silent exclusion** — the user who cannot enter their name, cannot pay, or cannot read the screen, and who leaves without ever complaining (§8) |
| The core team's obligation | **Published override protocol**: the core may overrule a locale decision, but must give written reasons to the same people who saw the decision, and override counts are reported quarterly beside locale metrics (§10) |
| Measurement | Behavioural instruments primary, per-locale trend only, **no cross-locale averaging of sentiment at all** (§11.2). Comparability method named, not promised (§11.3) |
| Failure test | Defined window, sample floor, variance test and **consequence**: Year 2 tranche not released (§11.4) |
| Investment sought | **$5.4M Year 1, $3.3M Year 2** (assumptions §14.1), of which **$1.6M is paid in-market review and research time** — the line most often cut and most often fatal |
| Benefit case | §14.2 — three markets unlocked, ~$8.1M of avoided remediation, three regulatory exposures retired |
| Decisions requested | **Five** — §15, sought at the council meeting on **4 June** |
| Owner | Head of Product, sponsor; **Localisation Architect** appointed within 30 days, sitting in engineering, not in marketing |

### 1.1 The core proposition, and how confident we are in it

Cultural inclusion is overwhelmingly an **architecture** problem, secondarily a **content governance** problem, and only marginally a matter of taste review. Products that get the architecture right can fix bad copy in an afternoon. Products that get it wrong cannot fix a name field without a data migration and a customer-communications exercise.

*(Considered practitioner assertion, not a research finding — evidence key at §16. We flag it because the council is entitled to know which statements here rest on evidence and which on our judgement.)*

The failure we are trying to avoid is documented in our own past work: a product shipped as a United States product with a language dropdown attached, then patched market by market until the codebase carries forty conditional branches that nobody dares touch. That outcome is worse than launching in fewer markets, because it consumes the engineering credibility a second attempt would need.

We note, and §5 addresses, the fair criticism that devolving as much as we propose could produce exactly those forty branches. Devolution without a variation discipline is not generosity to locales; it is an unfunded liability placed on engineering, and it would be the locale owners who were eventually blamed for it. That would be an unhappy outcome for ever
